title: Contra Duas Epistulas Pelegianorum
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa021.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: absit ergo, ut in libro meo contra haec testimonia diuina iste aliquid legerit; sed uel non intellegendo uel magis calumniando in alium sensum conatur detorquere quod legit. librum autem meum, contra quem se quattuor libellis respondisse commemorat, post damnationem Pelagii Caelestiique conscripsi. quod ideo dicendum putaui, quoniam iste dicit \'ab inimicis suis in odium ueritatis dicta mea fuisse suscepta\', ne ideo quisquam existimet propter hunc librum meum inimicos gratiae Christi nonos hereticos fuisse damnatos.
passages.english: Far be it, then, that this man should have read anything in my book against these divine testimonies; rather, either by not understanding or, more likely, by slandering, he tries to twist what he read into another sense. Now, my book, against which he mentions that he has replied in four little books, I wrote after the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius. I thought this should be said because he says that 'my words were taken up by his enemies out of hatred of the truth', so that no one should suppose that it was on account of this book of mine that the enemies of the grace of Christ were condemned as new heretics.

passages.original: sed per gratiam domini Iesu Christi credimus salui fieri quema d 111 o d u in et illi. hoc uos non uultis. inimici huic g-ratiae, ut eadem gratia Iesu Christi salui facti credantur antiqui, sed distribuitis tempora secundum Pelagium, in cuius libris hoc legitur, et ante legem dicitis saluos factos esse natura, deinde per legem, postremo per Christum, quasi hominibus duorum superiorum temporum, ante legem scilicet et in lege, sanguis Christi non fuerit necessarius, euacuantes quod dictum est: unus enim i m deus, unus et mediator dei et hominum homo Christus Iesus.
passages.english: 'But through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we believe that we are saved, just as they also [are].' This you do not want, enemies of this grace: that the ancients should be believed to have been saved by the same grace of Jesus Christ. Instead you divide up the ages following Pelagius, in whose books this is read, and you say that before the law [people] were saved by nature, then through the law, and finally through Christ, as if for the people of the two earlier ages, that is, before the law and under the law, the blood of Christ had not been necessary, making void what was said: 'For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.'
passages.notes: Garbled 'quema d 111 o d u in' read as 'quemadmodum'; 'g-ratiae' as 'gratiae'; stray 'i m' after 'unus enim' omitted.

passages.original: nunc illud est, quod debemus aduertere, utrum inuito et reluctanti homini deus inspiret boni cupiditatem, ut iam non sit reluctans, non sit inuitus, sed consentiens bono et uolens bonum. isti enim uolunt in homine ab ipso homine incipere cupiditatem boni, ut huius coepti meritum etiam perficiendi gratia consequatur. si tamen hoc saltem uolunt; Pelagius enim \'facilius\' dicit inpleri quod bonum est, si adiuuet gratia. quo additamento, id est addendo \'facilius\', utique significat hoc se sapere, quod, etiamsi gratiae defuerit adiutorium, potest quamuis difficilius inpleri bonum per liberum arbitrium.
passages.english: Now this is what we must consider: whether God inspires the desire for good in a person who is unwilling and resisting, so that he is no longer resisting, no longer unwilling, but consenting to the good and willing the good. For these men want the desire for good to begin in a person from the person himself, so that the merit of this beginning may also obtain the grace of completing [it]. If indeed they want even this much; for Pelagius says that what is good is fulfilled 'more easily' if grace helps. By this addition, that is, by adding 'more easily', he certainly indicates that this is his view: that even if the help of grace is lacking, the good can, though with more difficulty, be fulfilled through free choice.

passages.original: si enim sine dei gratia per nos incipit cupiditas boni, ipsum coeptum erit meritum, cui tamquam cx debito gratiae ueniat adiutorium, ac sic gratia dei non gratis donabitur, sed secundum meritum nostrum dabitur. dominus autem, ut responderet futuro Pelagio, non ait: \'sine me difficile potestis aliquid facere\', sed ait: sinc me nihil potestis facere. et ut responderet futuris etiam istis in eadem ipsa euangelica sententia, non ait: sine me nihil potestis \'perficere\', sed facere.
passages.english: For if the desire for good begins in us without the grace of God, that very beginning will be a merit, to which the help of grace comes as if by debt, and so the grace of God will not be given freely but will be given according to our merit. But the Lord, to answer the Pelagius who was to come, did not say, 'Without me you can do anything only with difficulty,' but said, 'Without me you can do nothing.' And to answer these men also who were to come, in that same gospel saying he did not say, 'Without me you can complete nothing,' but 'do'.

passages.original: quapropter utrosque damnat atque deuitat quisquis secundum regulam catholicae fidei sic in hominibus nascentibus de bona creatura carnis et animae glorificat creatorem — quod non uult Manicheus —, ut tamen propter uitium, quod in eos per peccatum primi hominis pertransiit, fateatur et paruulis necessarium saluatorem — quod non uult Pelagius —; sic discernit malum pudendae concupiscentiae a bonitate nuptiarum, ut neque Manicheis similis unde nascimur culpet neque Pelagi. anis similis unde confundimur laudet; sic legem per Moysen sanctam et iustam et bonam a deo sancto et iusto et bono datam esse defendit — quod contra apostolum negat Manicheus —, ut eam dicat et peccatum ostendere, non tamen tollere et iustitiam iubere, non tamen dare — quod rursus contra apostolum negat Pelagius -; sic asserit liberum arbitrium, ut non ex natura nescio qua semper mala, quae nulla est, sed ex ipso arbitrio coepisse dicat et angeli et hominis malum — quod euertit heresim Manicheam —, nec ideo tamen posse captiuam uoluntatem nisi dei gratia respirare in salubrem libertatem — quod euertit heresim Pelagianam —;
passages.english: Therefore whoever, according to the rule of the catholic faith, condemns and avoids both [heresies] is one who so glorifies the Creator for the good creation of flesh and soul in human beings at birth — which the Manichaean does not want — that he nevertheless confesses, on account of the fault which passed into them through the sin of the first man, that even infants need a saviour — which Pelagius does not want; who so distinguishes the evil of shameful concupiscence from the goodness of marriage that he neither, like the Manichaeans, blames that from which we are born, nor, like the Pelagians, praises that by which we are put to shame; who so defends that the law given through Moses was holy and just and good, given by a holy and just and good God — which the Manichaean denies, against the apostle — that he says it both shows sin yet does not take it away, and commands righteousness yet does not give it — which again Pelagius denies, against the apostle; who so affirms free choice that he says the evil of both angel and man began not from some nature or other that is always evil, which does not exist, but from choice itself — which overturns the Manichaean heresy — and yet that the captive will cannot, except by the grace of God, breathe again into saving freedom — which overturns the Pelagian heresy;
passages.notes: 'Pelagi. anis' read as 'Pelagianis'. The passage is a fragment of a longer sentence continuing beyond it.

passages.original: quodsi propterea non potest illis uerbis apostoli peccatum intellegi, in quo omnes peccauerunt, quia in graeco, unde translata est epistula, peccatum feminino genere positum est, restat, ut in illo primo homine peccasse omnes intellegantur, quia in illo fuerunt omnes quando ille peccauit, unde peccatum nascendo trahitur, quod nisi renascendo non soluitur. nam sic et sanctus Hilarius intellexit quod scriptum est: i n. quo omnes peccauerunt; ait enim: in quo, id est Adam omnes peccauerunt. deinde addidit: manifestum in Adam omnes peccasse quasi in massa; ipse enim per peccatum corruptus, omnes quos genuit nati sunt sub peccato. haec scribens Hilarius sine ambiguitate commonuit, quomodo intellegendum esset \'in quo omnes peccauerunt".
passages.english: But if, in those words of the apostle, "in which all sinned," sin cannot be understood because in the Greek, from which the epistle was translated, "sin" is set in the feminine gender, it remains that all are understood to have sinned in that first man, because all were in him when he sinned; from which sin is contracted by being born, which is not loosed except by being reborn. For so too holy Hilary understood what is written, "in which all sinned"; for he says: "In which, that is, in Adam, all sinned." Then he added: "It is manifest that all sinned in Adam as in a lump; for he himself, corrupted through sin, all whom he begot were born under sin." In writing these things Hilary pointed out without ambiguity how "in which all sinned" was to be understood.
passages.notes: The Greek relative (eph' hō) cannot refer to the feminine hamartia, so Augustine argues it refers to Adam. "quasi in massa": "as in a lump/mass" (of humanity). Hilary here is probably 'Hilary' as Augustine knew him (likely Ambrosiaster).

passages.original: Beatissimum, corona etiam martyrii gloriosissimum Cyprianum nec africanis atque occidentalibus tantum, uerum et orientalibus ecclesiis fama praedicante et scripta eius longe lateque diffundente notissimum etiam ipse heresiarcha istorum Pelagius cum debito certe honore commemorat, ubi Testimoniorum librum scribens eum sc asserit imitari \'hoc se\' dicens \'facere ad Romanum, quod ille fecerit ad Quirinum\'. uideamus ergo quid de originali peccato, quod per unum hominem intrauit in mundum, senserit Cyprianus.
passages.english: Cyprian, most blessed, and most glorious also by the crown of martyrdom, very well known not only to the African and Western but also to the Eastern churches, as fame proclaims him and spreads his writings far and wide, is mentioned with due honour, certainly, even by Pelagius himself, the arch-heretic of these men, where, writing a Book of Testimonies, he declares that he is imitating him, saying that 'he is doing for Romanus what that man did for Quirinus'. Let us see, then, what Cyprian thought about original sin, which entered the world through one man.
passages.notes: 'sc' read as 'se'. Romanus is otherwise unidentified here.

passages.original: respondeant Pelagiani, quando fuerimus in inmortalitate paradisi et quomodo inde fuerimus expulsi, ut eo Christi gratia reuocemur. et cum inuenire nequiuerint quid hic pro sua peruersitate respondeant, adtendant quemadmodum intellexerit Cyprianus quod ait apostolus: in quo omnes peccauerunt et Pelagiani heretici noui de Manicheis ueteribus hereticis nulli catholico audeant inrogare calumniam, ne tam sceleratam etiam martyri antiquo Cypriano facere conuincantur iniuriam.
passages.english: Let the Pelagians answer when we were in the immortality of paradise, and how we were expelled from there, so that we might be called back there by the grace of Christ. And when they are unable to find what to answer here on behalf of their perversity, let them attend to how Cyprian understood what the apostle says, "in which all sinned," and let the Pelagians, new heretics, not dare to bring the slanderous charge of the Manichees, old heretics, against any catholic, lest they be convicted of doing so wicked an injury even to the ancient martyr Cyprian.

passages.original: neque enim qui consuluerat inde dubitabat, utrum nascentes traherent originale peccatum, quod renascendo diluerent — absit enim ut hinc aliquando fides christiana dubitauerit I —, sed ille dubitabat, utrum regenerationis lauacrum, quo non dubitabat soluendum originale peccatum, ante diem tradi deberet octauum. ad quam consultationem respondens beatissimus Cyprianus: quantum uero, inquit, a d causam infantum pertinet, quos dixisti intra secundum uel tertium diem quam nati sunt constitutos baptizari non oportere et considerandam esse legem circumcisionis antiquae, ut intra octauum diem eum qui natus est baptizandum et sanctificandum non putares, longe aliud concilio nostro omni uisum est. in hoc enim quod putabas esse faciendum, nemo consensit, sed uniuer si potius iudicauimus nulli hominum nato misericordis dei gratiam denegandam. nam cum dominus in euangelio suo dicat : filius hominis non uenit animas perdere, sed saluare\', quantum in nobis est, si fieri potest, nulla anima perdenda est. et paulo post: nec aliquis, inquit, nostrum id debet horrere, quod dominus dignatus est facere. 11 nam etsi adhuc in infans a partu nouus est, non ita est tamen, ut quisquam illum in gratia danda a atque in pace facienda horrere debeat osculari, quando in osculo infantis unus quisque nostrum pro sua religione ipsas adhuc recentes dei manus debeat cogitare, quas in homine modo formato et recens nato quodammodo exosculamur, quando id quod deus exosculamur.
passages.english: For the one who had consulted him was not in doubt on this point, whether those being born contracted original sin, which they would wash away by being reborn — far be it that the Christian faith should ever have doubted this — but he was in doubt whether the bath of regeneration, by which he did not doubt original sin was to be loosed, ought to be given before the eighth day. Replying to this inquiry, the most blessed Cyprian says: "But as far as concerns the case of infants, who you said ought not to be baptized when within the second or third day after they are born, and that the law of the ancient circumcision should be considered, so that you thought one who is born should not be baptized and sanctified within the eighth day, something far different seemed right to our whole council. For no one agreed to what you thought should be done, but rather we all judged that the grace of the merciful God should be denied to no human being born. For since the Lord says in his Gospel, 'The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls but to save [them],' as far as lies in us, if it can be done, no soul is to be lost." And a little later: "Nor ought any of us," he says, "to shrink from what the Lord has deigned to do. For although the infant is still new from birth, it is not so that anyone ought to shrink from kissing him in giving grace and making peace, since in kissing an infant each one of us, according to his piety, ought to think of the very hands of God still fresh, which in a man just formed and newly born we in a certain manner kiss, when we kiss what God has made."
passages.notes: The final clause reads "quando id quod deus exosculamur", evidently missing a verb (likely "fecit"); translated as "what God has made". Stray marks ("11", "a") omitted as scanning artefacts.

passages.original: puto quod \'omnes prophetas et apostolos uel quoslibet sanctos, qui domino quocumque tempore placuerunt, non in conparatione sceleratorum\', sicut nos isti dicere calumniantur, \'sed regula uirtutum\', sicut se dicere gloriantur, \'iustos fuisse\' nouerat Cyprianus, qui tamen dicit: nemo esse sine peccato potest et quisque se inculpatum dixerit, aut superbus aut stultus est. nec propter aliud intellegit scriptum: quis gloriabitur castum se haberecor aut quis gloriabitur mundum se esse a peccatis? puto quod non ab istis docendus fuerat Cyprianus, quod optime sciebat, \'in futuro tempore mercedem esse bonorum operum, malorum autem supplicium;
passages.english: I suppose that Cyprian knew that "all the prophets and apostles, or any saints whatever who pleased the Lord at whatever time, were righteous not in comparison with the wicked," as these men slanderously say that we say, "but by the rule of the virtues," as they boast that they say; and yet he says: "No one can be without sin, and whoever says he is blameless is either proud or foolish." Nor for any other reason does he understand what is written: "Who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sins?" I suppose that Cyprian did not need to be taught by these men what he knew very well, that "in the time to come there is a reward for good works, but punishment for evil ones;

passages.original: Pelagiani dicunt ab homine incipere meritum per liberum arbitrium, cui deus subsequens gratiae retribuat adiumentum. etiam hic cos refellat uenerandus Ambrosius dicens in Expositione Esaiae prophetae: quia humana cura sine diuina ope inbecilla est ad medendum, deum auxiliatorem requirit. item in libro qui inscribitur De fuga saeculi: frequens nobis, inquit, de effugiendo saeculo isto sermo atque utinam quam facilis sermo tam cautus et sollicitus affectus!
passages.english: The Pelagians say that merit begins from man through free will, to which God, following after, repays the aid of grace. Here too let the venerable Ambrose refute them, saying in the Exposition of the Prophet Isaiah: "Because human care without divine help is too weak to heal, it seeks God as helper." Likewise in the book entitled On Flight from the World: "We often speak," he says, "of fleeing this world, and would that the disposition were as careful and anxious as the speech is easy!

passages.original: Nimis longum erit, si omnia uelim commemorare, quae sanctus Ambrosius aduersus hanc heresim Pelagianorum tanto post exorturam non eis quidem respondens, sed praedicans catholicam fidem atque in ea homines aedificans dixit et scripsit. sed nec illa omnia commemorare potui uel debui, quae gloriosissimus in domino Cyprianus posuit in epistulis suis, quibus demonstretur, quam sit haec, quam tenemus, fides uera uereque christiana atque catholica, sicut per scripturas sanctas antiquitus tradita sic a patribus nostris et usque ad hoc tempus, quo isti eam conuellere temptauerunt, retenta atque seruata et deinceps propitio deo retinenda atque seruanda.
passages.english: It would be too long if I wished to recount all the things that holy Ambrose said and wrote against this heresy of the Pelagians, which was to arise so long afterwards — not indeed answering them, but preaching the catholic faith and building people up in it. But neither could I nor should I recount all those things which Cyprian, most glorious in the Lord, set down in his letters, by which it may be shown how this faith which we hold is true and truly Christian and catholic: as it was handed down of old through the holy Scriptures, so it was kept and preserved by our fathers even up to this time, in which these men have tried to overthrow it, and henceforth, God being gracious, is to be kept and preserved.
